pages.text: Welcome Baseball Fans! | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Welcome Baseball Fans! If you're a fan of baseball and disability employment, you've come to the right place! At the U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP), we work to increase success for people with disabilities in America's workplaces. This is a goal we share with our Alliance partner the Professional Baseball Athletic Trainers Society (PBATS). Over the years, ODEP and PBATS have collaborated on a number of activities, including the production of several public service announcements (PSAs) featuring former MLB players with disabilities and/or professional baseball athletic trainers from clubs around the country. Among the topics these PSAs address is the importance of helping people stay at or return to work after injury or illness and, most recently, strategies for fostering mental health-friendly workplaces. Please view and share these PSAs and explore our resources for fostering supportive workplaces, for all workers in all types of workplaces—because everyone should be in the game. pages.text: We’ve Been Strapping Cargo to Our Backs for Millions of Years, but Backpack Innovation Really Took Off Around the Civil War Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via public domain Humans have been carting things on our backs in wraps of some kind at least since we began using tools, around two million years ago—and we have always sought ways to make the load more comfortable. The oldest known backpack ever discovered, in the Alps on the border between Austria and Italy, employed two narrow wooden boards and a hazel rod for a frame. The contraption dates to around 3300 B.C. and is credited to Ötzi the Iceman , a glacier mummy unearthed alongside it in 1991. But what we recognize as a backpack is much newer. In 1865, Henry Clay Merriam led a regiment of Black Union troops in an attack against Fort Blakely, a Confederate stronghold in Alabama. His deeds in this final battle of the Civil War earned him a Medal of Honor “for conspicuous gallantry.” Afterward, the lieutenant colonel had an epiphany: It was burdensome to carry both a knapsack (a pack with shoulder straps but no frame for internal support) and a haversack (a shoulder bag containing his rations). Based on his time carrying gear for the Army, Merriam devised a solution: a boxy canvas pack with room for socks, a quart of water, a shaving kit and a deck of cards, plus a compartment for rations in a case at the bottom. Credit: wing-wing/Shutterstock A day, as we all know, is 24 hours, also known as 1,440 minutes or 86,400 seconds. Or if you’re an atomic clock maker, exactly 794,243,384,928,000 cycles of microwave radiation tuned to the ticking rate of the cesium atom . Regardless, a day is a day, right? Actually, no: An Earth day isn’t a fixed interval of time. You may have noticed news stories reporting that Earth has shaved a millisecond (thousandth of a second) or more off the time it takes to make a full rotation, or conversely, that the planet’s rotation has slowed down slightly. While some of these stories exaggerate the impacts of these changes, their basic premise is correct: Earth’s seemingly steady rotation can, at times, seem as fickle as the weather. This wouldn’t be a problem — or even noticeable — except that we have two different ways of telling time that don’t quite agree with each other. The one that probably feels most intuitive is solar time, in which a day is defined by the time it takes our planet Earth to rotate once on its axis with respect to the Sun. These secret codes, known as ciphers, could be as simple as taking a message and shifting each letter of the alphabet by a certain number of positions so that A became D, B became E, etc. But cryptography has evolved greatly since these earliest examples. At the beginning of the third century B.C.E., Ptolemy I, successor to Alexander the Great, set out to build something the world had never before seen. The Macedonian general, probable bigamist , and body snatcher turned self-styled pharaoh wanted to make Alexandria the intellectual capital of the world. Having intercepted the corpse of Alexander the Great on its way home to Macedonia, he instead interred it in Alexandria to legitimize his rule. He attracted scholars with promises of royal patronage, dispatched scribes to copy texts from throughout the known world, and allegedly had agents search arriving ships for books. The result was the Library of Alexandria: antiquity’s most ambitious attempt to gather all human knowledge in one place. Then it went up in flames. Or so we’ve been told.
